5.4 Rejection frequencies and their interpretation

A well-calibrated nominal 5% test should reject approximately 5% of no-break datasets. Power must be interpreted alongside size: a method that rejects too often under the null can have misleadingly high apparent power.

method_names <- c(iid = "IID residual", wild = "Independent wild", dwb = "Dependent wild")
simulation_comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(sim$config), function(config) {
  z <- sim[sim$config == config, ]
  rates <- vapply(c("iid", "wild", "dwb"), function(method) {
    100 * z$rejection_rate[z$method == method]
  }, numeric(1L))
  data.frame(
    Configuration = config, Quantity = ifelse(z$delta[1] == 0, "Size", "Power"),
    Change = z$delta[1], Rho = z$rho[1],
    Innovation_scale = ifelse(z$heteroskedastic[1], "Increasing", "Constant"),
    IID_residual_percent = rates[1], Independent_wild_percent = rates[2],
    Dependent_wild_percent = rates[3], row.names = NULL
  )
}))
knitr::kable(simulation_comparison, digits = 1, caption = "Rejection frequencies (%)")

2 Power 0.1 0.0 Constant 100.0 100.0 99.0

With independent, constant-variance errors, IID residual and independent wild tests have sizes 4.1% and 4.3%. Under independence and increasing variance, IID residual size rises to 8.8%, while independent wild remains near nominal at 5.4%.

Serial correlation has a larger effect. At \(\rho=0.4\), the independent procedures reject 26.5–32.2% of no-break datasets across the scale designs. Their resampling schemes remove the serial dependence affecting the observed search statistic, making the simulated critical values too small in these settings.

DWB null rejection rates are 2.1–3.5%. It avoids over-rejection here but is conservative relative to 5%, rather than exactly calibrated. Its power is 98.5–99.0% under independence and 74.6–78.5% with autocorrelation. Higher apparent power from the independent methods under serial correlation should not be read as superior performance because their null sizes are distorted. Size-adjusted power is not calculated.

The simulation supports retaining dependence in station inference, but it does not prove that the empirical DWB p-value is conservative. It covers Gaussian innovations, one sample size, one reasonably strong central kink and one DWB bandwidth. It does not evaluate missingness, weak or multiple breaks, alternative dependence models or confidence-interval coverage. Those limits temper direct transfer to the irregular empirical record.

6 Conclusion

The Geneva record from 1753 to 2013 shows a positive average linear trend of 0.0337 °C per decade, but a single straight line is not an adequate description of it. The residuals of the linear model are positively autocorrelated (Monte Carlo Durbin–Watson p = 0.0002), while there is no evidence of a trend in the residual variance (Breusch–Pagan p = 0.5183). Part of this dependence reflects low-frequency movements that one slope cannot capture.

A continuous broken trend fits best with a kink at 1851 and reduces the residual sum of squares by 12.53%. It describes the record as a slightly declining trend before the break (-0.0525 °C per decade) followed by warming of 0.0887 °C per decade. The selected year coincides with the coldest year in the record, but excluding that year or the post-gap observations leaves the kink in the mid-nineteenth century, a timing consistent with the end of the Little Ice Age in the Alps.

The evidence that the trend actually changed is moderate. The primary dependent wild bootstrap rejects the no-break null at the 5% level (p = 0.0331), but its p-value rises with the bandwidth to 0.0541 at \(\ell=12\). Bootstrap procedures that ignore serial dependence reject much more strongly, but their p-values are not credible given the Section 3 diagnostics. Conditional on the broken-trend model, the pre-break slope is not distinguishable from zero, while the post-break slope is positive under both interval types.

The simulation study shows that independent-error bootstraps over-reject substantially when errors are autocorrelated, whereas the DWB keeps size at or below the nominal level at the cost of lower power. This supports the choice of the DWB for this station, although it does not prove that the empirical DWB p-value is conservative.

In answer to the research question, the Geneva record indicates warming since the mid-nineteenth century of about 0.89 °C per century; a single linear trend understates this warming by averaging it with an earlier cooler phase; and there is moderate, bandwidth-sensitive statistical evidence for a change in the trend. The main limitations are the missing years 1981–2009, station history beyond what homogenisation corrects, the restriction to a single break and a single dependence model, and the absence of a coverage study for the confidence intervals.

Appendix A: Computational validation

The checks below are executable rather than asserted. They compare the optimised break search with brute-force OLS, reconstruct both interval types from the stored bootstrap draws, verify the finite-replication p-value corrections, reconstruct every simulation rejection frequency and Wilson interval, and replay one complete dataset from each of the eight simulation scenarios. All functions used are defined in this document, and the checks write only to its working folder.

A.1 Section 3 computations

These checks verify that the 1850 centring and mean-year centring give identical fitted lines and slopes, that the complete supplied sample is retained, that an independent QR projection reproduces all 9,999 draws for both DW definitions, and that the BP statistic agrees with its one-regressor squared-correlation identity.

original_data <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv"))
stopifnot(identical(dat$Year, original_data$Year),
          identical(dat$Temperature, original_data$Temperature),
          n == 226L, length(missing_years) == 35L, nrow(gap_table) == 5L)
centered_model <- lm(Temperature ~ I((Year - mean(Year)) / 10), data = dat)
stopifnot(max(abs(fitted(centered_model) - fitted(trend_model))) < 1e-10,
          abs(coef(centered_model)[2] - beta1_hat) < 1e-12,
          abs(coef(centered_model)[1] + beta1_hat * (1850 - mean(dat$Year)) / 10 - beta0_hat) < 1e-12)

set.seed(master_seed)
Z_check <- matrix(rnorm(n * B), nrow = n)
Q_check <- qr.Q(qr(model.matrix(trend_model)))
E_check <- Z_check - Q_check %*% crossprod(Q_check, Z_check)
dw_replayed <- colSums((E_check[-1, , drop = FALSE] -
                        E_check[-n, , drop = FALSE])^2) / colSums(E_check^2)
dw_gap_replayed <- colSums((E_check[valid_pairs + 1L, , drop = FALSE] -
                            E_check[valid_pairs, , drop = FALSE])^2) / colSums(E_check^2)
stopifnot(max(abs(dw_replayed - d_sim)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(dw_gap_replayed - d_sim_gap)) < 1e-10,
          abs(n * cor(dat$residual_sq, dat$t)^2 - BP_stat) < 1e-12)

  "PASS: all supplied rows, five gaps and 35 missing years are retained",
  "PASS: year-1850 and mean-year parameterizations have identical fitted lines and slopes",
  "PASS: independent QR projection reproduces both 9,999-draw DW reference distributions",
  "PASS: BP agrees with the one-regressor squared-correlation identity"
)

A.2 Break search, intervals and simulation

checks <- character()
pass <- function(text) {
  checks <<- c(checks, paste("PASS:", text))
  cat(tail(checks, 1L), "\n")
}
station <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv"))
stopifnot(nrow(station) == 226L, !anyNA(station),
          !anyDuplicated(station$Year), all(diff(station$Year) > 0))
y <- station$Temperature
D <- prepare_design(station$Year)
fitted_break <- fit_break(y, D)
x <- D$x
rss_grid <- sapply(D$index, function(k)
  deviance(lm(y ~ x + I(pmax(0, x - x[k])))))
rss_null <- deviance(lm(y ~ x))
stopifnot(abs(fitted_break$F - (rss_null - min(rss_grid))) < 1e-9,
          fitted_break$index == D$index[which.min(rss_grid)],
          max(abs(fitted_break$fitted - fitted(lm(y ~ x +
            I(pmax(0, x - x[fitted_break$index])))))) < 1e-9)
pass("optimized break search agrees with independent brute-force OLS and fitted values")
## PASS: optimized break search agrees with independent brute-force OLS and fitted values
set.seed(320926)
for (method in c("iid", "wild", "dwb")) {
  errors <- bootstrap_errors(fitted_break$null_residuals, D$year, 7L, method, 6, 2)
  projected <- break_statistics(errors, D)$F
  brute <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(errors)), function(b) {
    ystar <- fitted_break$null_fitted + errors[, b]
    rss0 <- deviance(lm(ystar ~ x))
    rss1 <- min(sapply(D$index, function(k)
      deviance(lm(ystar ~ x + I(pmax(0, x - x[k]))))))
    rss0 - rss1
  }, numeric(1L))
  stopifnot(max(abs(projected - brute)) < 1e-8)
}

for (parameter in c("pre", "post")) {

  pt <- ci[ci$parameter == parameter & ci$type == "percentile_t", ]
  draws <- ci_draws[[parameter]]
  ses <- ci_draws[[paste0("se_", parameter)]]
  stopifnot(all(ses > 0), all(is.finite(ses)))
  percentile <- quantile(draws, c(.025, .975), type = 7, names = FALSE)

  studentized <- pt$estimate - pt$hac_se *
    quantile(tstar, c(.975, .025), type = 7, names = FALSE)
  stopifnot(max(abs(percentile - c(pc$lower, pc$upper))) < 1e-10,
            max(abs(studentized - c(pt$lower, pt$upper))) < 1e-10)
}

  one <- raw[raw$config == s, ]
  stopifnot(identical(sort(as.integer(one$replication)), seq_len(1000L)),
            all(one$replicate_seed == 20260926L + s * 100000L + one$replication))
  for (method in c("iid", "wild", "dwb")) {

      abs(row$mc_se - sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / 1000)) < 1e-12,
      max(abs(c(row$lower_95, row$upper_95) - interval)) < 1e-12)
  }
}
pass("all 8,000 replications, 24 rejection rates, MC standard errors and Wilson intervals are consistent")
## PASS: all 8,000 replications, 24 rejection rates, MC standard errors and Wilson intervals are consistent
# Replay one observation from every scenario, independently of worker scheduling.
Ds <- prepare_design(seq_len(226L))
for (s in seq_len(8L)) {
  row <- raw[raw$config == s & raw$replication == 1000L, ]
  set.seed(row$replicate_seed)
  ys <- simulate_broken_trend(Ds, row$delta, row$rho, row$heteroskedastic,
                              simulation$settings$sigma)
  result <- bootstrap_break(ys, Ds, B = 499L)
  stopifnot(abs(result$observed$F - row$F) < 1e-10)
  for (method in c("iid", "wild", "dwb"))
    stopifnot(abs(result$results[[method]]$p_value - row[[paste0(method, "_p")]]) < 1e-12)
}
pass("recorded seeds reproduce one complete replication from every simulation scenario")
## PASS: recorded seeds reproduce one complete replication from every simulation scenario
writeLines(checks, "outputs/validation.txt")
cat("All checks passed. Saved outputs/validation.txt.\n")
## All checks passed. Saved outputs/validation.txt.

Appendix B: Random seeds and session information

The Section 3 Monte Carlo test and its replay in Appendix A use seed 20260926. The empirical IID residual, independent wild and primary DWB tests use the master seed 20260926 plus 101, 102 and 103. The bandwidth checks use the master seed plus 203 and 212, and the slope intervals use the master seed plus 301. Simulation dataset \(m\) in scenario \(c\) uses 20260926 + 100000*c + m, independently of worker scheduling.

Appendix C: Choice of reference year

The time index is \(t=(\mathrm{Year}-1850)/10\); the division by ten reports slopes per decade. The reference year 1850 was chosen because it lies next to the estimated break date. The intercept of the linear model is then the fitted temperature in 1850, and, since the estimated break (1851) does not precede 1850, the intercept of the broken-trend model is also its fitted temperature in 1850. The two intercepts are thus directly comparable at 1850. The fitted level at the estimated turning point is instead \(\widehat\alpha+\widehat\beta(\widehat T_1-1850)/10\).

Any other reference year, such as the sample mean, would change only the intercept. Fitted values, residuals, slopes, the RSS, the break search and all test statistics are invariant, as verified in Appendix A.1. Centring at the sample mean would minimise the classical OLS variance of the intercept, but no inference in this report concerns the intercept. Because 1850 was chosen with knowledge of the Section 4 estimate, the choice is purely presentational; although 1850 is also a common pre-industrial reference year in climate assessments, it is not used here in that sense.

Appendix D: Effect of data gaps on the analysis

Component Effect of gaps Approach retained or refined
Exploratory and residual time plots Observed lines must not imply data inside gaps Lines are grouped by contiguous years; the largest gap is shaded
OLS estimates Calendar spacing is represented, but coverage and missingness can matter Retain \((\mathrm{Year}-1850)/10\) and the complete supplied sample
Residual ACF Observation lags and calendar lags differ Display both; calendar grid contains NA for absent years
Variance smooth Its curve inside a gap is unsupported by observations there Retain the descriptive smooth with an explicit limitation
QQ plot Time order is absent from its construction Treat it as a marginal descriptive comparison, not proof of Gaussianity
DW statistic and Monte Carlo The specified formula uses observation adjacency Primary specified statistic plus separately calibrated calendar-adjacent sensitivity
BP test Algebra uses actual time; dependence qualifies its reference Retain \(nR^2\) and nominal \(\chi^2_1\), with cautious non-rejection language
Section 4 bootstrap Dependence should use actual calendar gaps DWB multipliers depend on elapsed years; every sample repeats the date search
Overall interpretation Missing decades and metadata limit conclusions No inference about an unobserved trajectory, global change or physical cause
